references.text: This verse is almost identical to Exodus 15:21. Moses and the children of Israel sing the same song that Miriam repeats here, with the words 'Sing to the Lord, for he is highly exalted; the horse and its rider he has thrown into the sea.'
Describes the actual event where the Lord threw the Egyptians and their horses and riders into the sea, which Miriam's song celebrates.
The immediate context in which Miriam, the prophetess, takes the tambourine and leads the women in dance before she sings this song.
The psalm celebrates the same event: 'But Pharaoh and his army he cast into the Red Sea,' and praises the Lord's mighty deeds.
Recalls Israel's deliverance at the Red Sea and how the people believed in the Lord's word and sang his praise.
Revelation refers to 'the song of Moses, the servant of God,' linking back to this triumphal song by the sea.
Highlights how song and liturgy function as a strategic and theological part of Israel's warfare before and after victory.
Isaiah extends the historical deliverance at the sea into a cosmic hymn of praise over God's redemption of Jacob.
